div.p: Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (SATB2) is a nuclear matrixassociated protein with a pivotal role in glioblastoma (GBM) progression. However, the mechanisms underpinning aberrant SATB2 expression remain elusive. Here, we identify the ubiquitin specific peptidase 10 (USP10) as a deubiquitinase and the deltex E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 L (DTX3L) as a ubiquitin ligase of SATB2 in glioma stem cells (GSCs). USP10 and DTX3L regulate SATB2 ubiquitination at the K266 residue through mutually exclusive interactions and opposing activities. USP10, enriched in GSCs, is induced by transcription factor YY2. Knockdown of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L markedly downregulates SATB2, resulting in the inhibition of GSC self-renewal and GBM growth, which can be rescued by the overexpression of SATB2. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of USP10 by Wu-5 effectively suppresses tumor growth. These findings highlight the antagonistic roles of USP10 and DTX3L in the regulation of GBM malignancy and propose USP10 as a potential therapeutic target.

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and devastating brain tumor in adults. The standard therapy for GBM is surgery followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Despite remarkable progress in the treatment of other solid tumors, the prognosis for GBM patients remains bleak, with the median survival of GBM patients remains less than 16 months 1,2 . The malignant features of GBM are thought to be attributable to glioma stem cells (GSCs), a fraction of stem cell-like cancer cells that possess extraordinary capabilities for rapid proliferation, self-renewal, and tumorigenesis 3-5 . These GSCs have been shown to play a significant role in the initiation, progression, recurrence and resistance to therapy of GBM [6][7][8][9] . Therefore, the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting GSCs could provide significant insights that may enhance the efficacy of GBM treatments.

Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (SATB2) is a nuclear matrix-associated transcriptional factor that interacts with the nuclear matrix attachment regions of DNA, thereby regulating chromatin remodeling and gene transcription [10][11][12] . SATB2 recruits chromatinremodeling proteins to the matrix attachment regions, either to activate or repress gene transcription 11,13,14 . This protein has been shown to play a crucial role in the progression of various cancer types, including hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, prostate cancer, triplenegative breast cancer, and others [15][16][17][18] . In GBM, SATB2 is overexpressed in GBM tissues when compared to low-grade gliomas, and it is predominantly enriched in GSCs 19 . Disruption of SATB2 significantly suppresses GSC proliferation and self-renewal 19 . Moreover, SATB2 plays a key role in the progression of GBM and significantly contributes to the development of resistance to temozolomide and radiation therapy 19,20 . However, the precise mechanisms underlying SATB2 dysregulation in GSCs remain unclear.

The ubiquitin-proteasome system constitutes the primary pathway for non-lysosomal proteolysis of intracellular proteins and is accountable for the degradation of more than 80% of cellular proteins 21,22 . Ubiquitination, which is a process that marks proteins for degradation, plays a crucial supportive role in this regulatory mechanism 23 . This process is reversible and can be mediated by a diverse group of enzymes known as deubiquitylating enzymes, or termed deubiquitinases 24,25 . USP10, a member of ubiquitin-specific protease (USP) family, is one such deubiquitinase 26 . It has been implicated in the development of various cancer types, including triplenegative breast cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and others [27][28][29] . Recent studies have indicated that disruption of USP10 can induce apoptosis in GBM cells and suppress proneural-to-mesenchymal transition, a critical process in GBM progression 30,31 . Deltex E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 L (DTX3L) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase belonging to the deltex family 32 . This protein is associated with the occurrence and development of various cancer types, such as pancreatic cancer, cervical carcinoma, prostate cancer, and others [33][34][35] . However, the functional roles of USP10 and DTX3L in GSC biology remain largely enigmatic.

In this study, we identify that deubiquitinase USP10 and E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L function in concert to regulate the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2. Our data reveal that USP10 antagonizes DTX3Lmediated ubiquitination at the K266 residue, thereby stabilizing the SATB2 protein, which in turn contributes to the malignant phenotype of GSCs and the growth of GBM tumors. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of USP10 by a small molecule inhibitor, Wu-5, promotes SATB2 ubiquitination and thereby suppresses GSC proliferation, selfrenewal, and tumor growth. These findings indicate that USP10 could be a promising target for patients with GBM.

div.head: USP10 and DTX3L interact with SATB2 in GSCs
div.p: To determine whether the SATB2 protein is degraded through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway or the lysosomal degradation pathway, we first checked the SATB2 protein levels in two patient-derived GSCs after blocked de novo protein synthesis using cycloheximide (CHX). GSCs were functionally validated as described in Methods. We found the SATB2 protein levels were decreased in a time-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 1a). On the contrary, the protein levels of SATB2 were gradually increased after treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Supplementary Fig. 1b). However, the protein levels of SATB2 remained unchanged after treatment with the lysosome inhibitor Bafilomycin A1 (Supplementary Fig. 1c). These results indicate that the degradation of SATB2 is mediated through the ubiquitinproteasome system. To identify the potential deubiquitinases and ubiquitin ligases that regulate the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2, we performed mass spectrometry to analyze the SATB2-interacting proteins pulled down by the anti-Myc antibody from GSCs overexpressing Myc-tagged SATB2. Notably, among the top candidates of potential SATB2 binding partners, we identified the deubiquitinase USP10 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L (Fig. 1a, b

div.head: and Supplementary Table. 1).
div.p: To validate the interactions between SATB2 and either USP10 or DTX3L, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP) experiments in HEK293T cells that were co-expressing SATB2 with a Myc tag and either USP10 or DTX3L with a Flag tag. CoIP assay revealed that exogenous USP10 or DTX3L was readily detected in exogenous SATB2 pull-down complexes and vice versa (Fig. 1c-f). These interactions were confirmed by showing that endogenous USP10 or DTX3L could be detected in immunoprecipitates of endogenous SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 1g). To determine the specific region required for SATB2-USP10 or SATB2-DTX3L interaction, we generated various truncated mutants of SATB2-Myc, USP10-Flag, and DTX3L-Flag (Fig. 1h-j). CoIP assay showed that the central domain of SATB2 (amino acids 232-437) and the C-terminal USP domain of USP10 (amino acids 401-798) are required for interaction with each other (Fig. 1k, l). In addition, our results also showed that the central domain of SATB2 (amino acids 232-437) and the central domain of DTX3L (amino acids 201-554) are necessary for their interaction (Fig. 1m, n). Taken together, these data suggest that deubiquitinase USP10 and E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L interact with SATB2 in GSCs, suggesting that USP10 and DTX3L may regulate SATB2 stability.

div.head: USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed by GSCs
div.p: Considering that SATB2 is reported to be preferentially expressed by GSCs 19,20 , we subsequently aimed to verify if USP10 and DTX3L are also predominantly expressed by GSCs within GBM. We initially examined the protein expression of USP10 and DTX3L in five pairs of matched GSCs and non-stem tumor cells (NSTCs). Immunoblot (IB) analysis showed that USP10 and DTX3L were preferentially expressed in GSCs compared with matched NSTCs (Fig. 2a). In addition, the enrichment of SATB2 in GSCs, as shown in Fig. 2a, aligns with the results of our previous study 19 . Moreover, qPCR analysis also revealed that the mRNA levels of USP10 and DTX3L were expressed at much higher levels in GSCs than in NSTCs (Fig. 2b, c). We next compared the expression between USP10 and DTX3L and the results showed that the expression of USP10 was significantly higher than DTX3L in GSCs (Fig. 2d). As deubiquitinase and E3 ubiquitin ligase exert antagonistic effects on protein stability, the higher expression of USP10 than DTX3L may account for the abundant expression of SATB2 in GSCs. Immunofluorescent staining revealed that USP10 and DTX3L were predominantly located in the cytoplasm, while SATB2 was primarily found in the nuclei in GSCs (Fig. 2e, f). This observation suggests that the cytoplasmic SATB2 may be translocated to the nucleus after deubiquitination. To verify this hypothesis, we first performed immunofluorescent staining of SATB2 in GSCs after treatment with MG-132 or DMSO. The results showed that MG-132 treatment induced nuclear export of SATB2 in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the ubiquitination assay detected ubiquitination of SATB2 in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus (Supplementary Fig. 1e). These results confirm that the cytoplasmic SATB2 is translocated to the nucleus following deubiquitination. Subsequently, to confirm the preferentially expression of USP10 and DTX3L by GSCs in GBM, we examined the expression pattern of USP10 and DTX3L in several human GBM tumors. Our data confirmed that USP10 and DTX3L were preferentially expressed in glioma cells expressing the GSC marker SOX2 (Fig. 2g, h and Supplementary Fig. 1f, g). Furthermore, USP10 and DTX3L were both co-localized with SATB2 in human primary GBMs (Fig. 2i, j and Supplementary Fig. 1h, i). Collectively, these data demonstrate that both USP10 and DTX3L are preferentially expressed by GSCs in human GBM tumors.

div.head: USP10 is required for GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth
div.p: As USP10 is enriched in GSCs, we therefore explored the role of USP10 in GSC maintenance and GSC-driven tumor growth by using two independent shRNAs targeting USP10. As expected, lentiviralmediated expression of two independent USP10 shRNAs significantly reduced USP10 protein levels in GSCs, which also induced a notable decrease of SATB2 protein levels (Fig. 3a). However, the mRNA levels of SATB2 remained unchanged after USP10 disruption (Fig. 3b). In contrast, SATB2 disruption did not alter USP10 mRNA or protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Immunofluorescent staining also revealed that disruption of USP10 induced nuclear export of endogenous SATB2, which is consistent with our prediction (Supplementary Fig. 2c). We therefore investigated the impact of USP10 disruption on FOXM1 expression in GSCs, our results demonstrated that disrupting USP10 also reduced the mRNA and protein expression of FOXM1 (Supplementary Fig. 2d, e). However, this intervention had no effect on the expression of DTX3L (Supplementary Fig. 2d, e). As SATB2 is crucial for GSC maintenance, reduced expression of SATB2 protein by USP10 disruption may impact GSC functions. Our data demonstrated that silencing USP10 markedly inhibited GSC growth as detected by cell titer assay and reduced DNA replication as assayed by EdU incorporation assay (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 2f, g). In contrast, silencing USP10 had little effect on the growth of NSTCs (Supplementary Fig. 2h, i). Silencing USP10 also impaired GSC self-renewal as assessed by tumorsphere formation and in vitro limiting dilution assays (Fig. 3d-g). Consistently, silencing USP10 decreased the expression of the GSC marker SOX2 (Supplementary Fig. 2j). To verify whether the deubiquitinase activity of USP10 is required for GSC functions, we examined whether ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) or catalytically inactive mutant (C424A, CA) of USP10 could rescue the effects caused by USP10 disruption. We employed an additional USP10 shRNA that specifically targets the 3' UTR of the endogenous USP10 mRNA (designated as shUSP10-3') to achieve the knockdown of USP10 expression; thus, we were able to simultaneously silence endogenous USP10 and overexpress exogenous USP10 in GSCs. IB analysis showed that WT USP10, but not CA mutant, could rescue the decreased SATB2 protein levels caused by knockdown of endogenous USP10 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). In addition, ectopic expression of WT USP10, but not CA mutant, rescued the impaired GSC proliferation and self-renewal caused by endogenous USP10 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 3b-f). These results demonstrate that USP10 regulates SATB2 protein levels and GSC functions through its deubiquitinase activity.

To investigate the influence of USP10 on GSC-driven tumor growth in vivo, GSCs expressing shNT or shUSP10 were intracranially injected into the brains of immunodeficient mice. Animals bearing xenografts derived from GSCs expressing shUSP10 displayed extended survival and reduced tumor volumes than the control group (Fig. 3h, i). Immunofluorescent staining of Ki67 and SOX2 also demonstrated that disruption of USP10 markedly inhibited cell proliferation and reduced GSC population in GBM xenografts (Fig. 3j-m). Additionally, immunofluorescent staining of neuronal markers (MAP2 and TUBB3) and the astrocyte marker (GFAP) revealed that disruption of USP10 significantly increased the number of MAP2-, TUBB3-, and GFAP-positive cells (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). This finding demonstrates that USP10 disruption promotes the differentiation of GSCs in GBM xenografts. Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining confirmed a marked reduction in USP10 and SATB2 expression in xenografts expressing shUSP10 (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Collectively, our data demonstrate that USP10 plays a critical role in promoting GSC selfrenewal and GSC-driven tumor growth.

div.head: DTX3L impairs GSC self-renewal and GBM tumor growth
div.p: As the expression of DTX3L is much lower than USP10 in GSCs, we examined the role of DTX3L in GSCs by overexpressing of DTX3L. We found that overexpression of DTX3L reduced SATB2 protein levels, but this overexpression had no effect on SATB2 mRNA levels (Fig. 4a, b). In addition, the overexpression of DTX3L led to a reduction in FOXM1 expression, whereas it had no significant impact on USP10 expression and ubiquitination (Supplementary Fig. 5a-c). Based on these findings, we hypothesized that DTX3L may also exert an influence on GSC functions. Our results showed that overexpression of DTX3L significantly suppressed GSC growth and reduced DNA replication (Fig. 4c-e). Tumorsphere formation and in vitro limiting dilution assays demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L impaired GSC selfrenewal (Fig. 4f-i). Consistently, DTX3L overexpression also decreased the expression of SOX2 (Supplementary Fig. 5d). We also examined whether the DTX3L mutant (C561S and C564S, 2CS), which lacks E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, could regulate SATB2 protein levels and GSC functions. IB analysis indicated that overexpression of DTX3L 2CS did not result in the inhibition of SATB2 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 5e). Moreover, DTX3L 2CS overexpression had only a weak promoting effect on ubiquitination of SATB2 (Supplementary Fig. 5f, g). Consistently, it showed no significant impact on GSC proliferation and self-renewal (Supplementary Fig. 5h-l). We subsequently investigated whether the overexpression of DTX3L influenced GSC-driven tumor growth in mouse brains. The results showed that mice bearing tumors derived from DTX3L overexpressing GSCs showed extended survival and reduced tumor masses (Fig. 4j, k). Additionally, tumors derived from DTX3L-overexpressing GSCs contained much fewer proliferative cells and GSC populations than those of the control tumors (Fig. 4l-o). Furthermore, DTX3L overexpression markedly promoted the differentiation of GSCs in GBM xenografts, as indicated by immunofluorescence of MAP2, TUBB3, and GFAP (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Immunofluorescent analysis further confirmed that DTX3L expression was elevated and SATB2 levels were reduced in xenografts derived from DTX3L-overexpressing GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Taken together, we conclude that DTX3L exerts inhibitory effects on GSC self-renewal and GBM growth.

div.head: DTX3L ubiquitinates SATB2, whereas USP10 mediates SATB2 deubiquitination
div.p: Our results have demonstrated that the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L reduced the protein levels of SATB2, while the deubiquitinase USP10 was responsible for preserving SATB2 protein levels. To investigate the impact of DTX3L or USP10 on SATB2 protein stability, DTX3Loverexpressing or USP10 silencing GSCs were subjected to CHX treatment. IB analysis demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L or disruption of USP10 led to destabilization of the SATB2 protein (Fig. 5a-d and Supplementary Fig. 7a-d). Given that SATB2 is degraded through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, we sought to verify that DTX3L and USP10 regulate the turnover of SATB2 via the ubiquitinproteasome pathway. The results showed that MG-132 treatments inhibited the decreased protein levels of SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression or USP10 disruption (Fig. 5e, f). These data indicate that DTX3L and USP10 regulate SATB2 stability in a proteasomedependent manner. These results indicate that DTX3L promotes K48-linked polyubiquitination of SATB2, whereas USP10 prevents this polyubiquitination type of SATB2. We therefore co-expressed DTX3L-HA and USP10-Flag with SATB2-Myc in HEK293T cells and the result showed that overexpression of USP10 suppressed the interaction between SATB2 and DTX3L (Supplementary Fig. 7e). To confirm whether DTX3L and USP10 indeed function as an opposing pair of E3 ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase to regulate SATB2 ubiquitination and stability, we first co-expressed SATB2-Myc, DTX3L-HA, USP10-Flag with His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. CoIP assay revealed that overexpression of USP10 significantly reduced the ubiquitination of SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression (Supplementary Fig. 7h). Overexpression of USP10 also reduced the ubiquitination of endogenous SATB2 induced by DTX3L overexpression in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7i, j). Furthermore, silencing DTX3L decreased the ubiquitination of endogenous SATB2 induced by USP10 disruption in GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 7k, l). In vitro ubiquitination assays demonstrated that DTX3L directly promoted the ubiquitination of SATB2 (Supplementary Fig. 7m), whereas USP10 antagonized DTX3Lmediated SATB2 ubiquitination (Supplementary Fig. 7n). Functionally, overexpression of both DTX3L and USP10 prevented the inhibitory effect on GSC growth that was induced by DTX3L overexpression alone (Supplementary Fig. 7o). Conversely, simultaneous disruption of both DTX3L and USP10 attenuated the inhibitory effect on GSC growth that was triggered by USP10 disruption alone as well (Supplementary Fig. 7p). Collectively, we conclude that deubiquitinase USP10 maintains the protein levels of SATB2 by antagonizing DTX3L-mediated ubiquitination.

div.head: Overexpression of SATB2 rescues the effects caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression
div.p: Given that disruption of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L reduced SATB2 protein levels, we next explored whether exogenous overexpression of SATB2 could rescue the effects induced by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression. The reduction in SATB2 levels caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression was corrected to match the levels of endogenous SATB2 in the control group by introducing additional SATB2 through exogenous overexpression (Fig. 6a, b and Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). Exogenous overexpression of SATB2 rescued the impaired GSC proliferation and self-renewal caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6c-h and Supplementary Fig. 8c-j). Importantly, overexpression of SATB2 largely attenuated the increased survival of mice bearing xenografts derived from USP10 silencing or DTX3L overexpressing GSCs (Fig. 6i, j and Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). Consistently, overexpression of SATB2 restored the GSC-driven tumor growth impaired by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6k, l and Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining confirmed that overexpression of SATB2 restored in vivo cell proliferation impaired by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression, and rescued the reduced GSC population caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression (Fig. 6m-p and Supplementary Fig. 9e-h). Taken together, these data demonstrate that overexpression of SATB2 is able to rescue the effects caused by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression, indicating that USP10 and DTX3L regulate GSC self-renewal and GSC-driven tumor growth by controlling the protein levels of SATB2.

div.head: USP10 and DTX3L co-regulate the ubiquitination of SATB2 at K266
div.p: To pinpoint the lysine residues within human SATB2 protein that are regulated by USP10 or DTX3L, we generated a series of truncated SATB2 mutants and introduced them into HEK293T cells. Notably, among the various mutants, only the expression of the SATB2 mutant encompassing amino acids 232 to 437 exhibited a significant increase in response to USP10 overexpression (Fig. 7a). In addition, overexpression of DTX3L also inhibited the expression of this SATB2 mutant (amino acids 232-437), without affecting the expression of other mutants (Fig. 7b). Subsequently, we individually mutated all lysine residues within the SATB2 mutant (amino acids 232-437) to arginine. The results revealed that the SATB2-K266R mutant was uniquely unaffected by the overexpression of USP10 or DTX3L (Fig. 7c,d). Protein sequence alignment analysis revealed that the domain containing K266 within SATB2 protein is highly conserved across seven distinct species (Fig. 7e). To confirm the ubiquitination site of SATB2, we performed mass spectrometry to analyze the immunoprecipitated SATB2 proteins from HEK293T cells coexpressing SATB2-Myc and His-ubiquitin. The results showed that ubiquitin moieties were exclusively detected on residue K266 (Fig. 7f), confirming that the K266 site is the ubiquitination site of SATB2. To ascertain whether K266 of SATB2 is regulated by USP10 or DTX3L in GSCs, we mutated K266 within the full-length SATB2 and introduced this mutant into GSCs. The results confirmed that the expression of the SATB2-K266R mutant was unaffected by USP10 disruption or DTX3L overexpression in GSCs (Fig. 7g-j). Additionally, to verify whether DTX3L directly catalyzes the ubiquitination of SATB2 at the K266 residue, we co-expressed Myc-tagged WT SATB2 or K266R (KR) mutant SATB2 with DTX3L-Flag and His-ubiquitin in HEK293T cells. CoIP experiment demonstrated that overexpression of DTX3L promoted SATB2 ubiquitination, while it had no obvious effect on the ubiquitination of SATB2-K266R mutant (Fig. 7k). div.head: USP10 inhibitor Wu-5 suppresses GSC self-renewal and GSCdriven tumor growth
div.p: To evaluate the therapeutic potential of USP10 in GBM, we investigated whether pharmacologic inhibition of USP10 by a small molecule inhibitor named Wu-5 could impact GSCs and GSC-driven tumor growth. Cell viability assay revealed that 8 and 16 μM Wu-5 dosedependently inhibited GSC growth, whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4 μM) showed no significant effect (Fig. 8a). Wu-5 treatment also impaired GSC self-renewal and downregulated SOX2 expression in a dose-dependent manner (8 and 16 μM) (Fig. 8b-e and Supplementary Fig. 11a). Furthermore, Wu-5 (8 and 16 μM) dose-dependently induced GSC apoptosis, as demonstrated by the elevated levels of apoptotic markers Cleaved Caspase-7 and Cleaved PARP (Supplementary Fig. 11b). As expected, Wu-5 treatment reduced SATB2 protein levels in a dose-and time-dependent manner (Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 11c). We also observed that Wu-5 treatment reduced USP10 protein levels in a dose-and time-dependent manner (Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 11c), which is in line with the findings from previous research 37,38 . Nonetheless, treatment with 8 and 16 μM Wu-5 had no impact on SATB2 and USP10 mRNA levels (Fig. 8g and Supplementary Fig. 11d). Consistently, Wu-5 treatment at 8 and 16 μM dosedependently increased the ubiquitination of SATB2 in GSCs (Fig. 8h).

To determine whether SATB2 overexpression can rescue the effects of Wu-5 treatment on GSC maintenance, we transduced GSCs with SATB2-Myc and treated them with Wu-5 (16 μM). IB analysis showed that ectopic SATB2 expression restored SATB2 to endogenous levels, which had been reduced by Wu-5 treatment (Supplementary Fig. 11e). Importantly, restoring SATB2 to endogenous levels significantly rescued the Wu-5-induced impairment of GSC proliferation and selfrenewal (Supplementary Fig. 11f-j). These data indicate that Wu-5 treatment inhibits GSC maintenance via the USP10-SATB2 axis. We then assessed the therapeutic effects of Wu-5 on mice bearing GSCderived xenografts. Consistent with our in vitro findings, Wu-5 treatment effectively prolonged the survival of mice bearing GSC-derived tumors and reduced tumor volumes in mouse brains (Fig. 8i-k). Notably, no significant alterations in body weight were observed throughout the treatment period (Supplementary Fig. 12a, b). Wu-5 administration also significantly reduced Ki67-positive proliferative cells and SOX2-positive GSC populations in tumors (Fig. 8l-o). Moreover, immunofluorescent staining for MAP2, TUBB3, and GFAP revealed that Wu-5 robustly promoted GSC differentiation in GBM xenografts (Supplementary Fig. 12c-f). Additionally, Wu-5 treatment reduced SATB2 and USP10 in xenografts (Supplementary Fig. 12g-j).

To confirm whether Wu-5 can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, we intraperitoneally administered Wu-5 or DMSO to BALB/c nude mice and subsequently detected Wu-5 in mouse brain tissues by LC-MS/MS. The results demonstrated that Wu-5 concentrations reached an average of 673 ng/g tissue in the brains of mice treated with Wu-5 for 2 hours, whereas Wu-5 levels were very low and nearly undetectable in the brains of DMSO-treated controls (Supplementary Fig. 12k). Together, these data suggest that pharmacological inhibition of USP10 significantly suppresses GSC self-renewal and tumor growth via promoting SATB2 destabilization, suggesting that that targeting USP10 may effectively improve GBM treatment.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: As a nuclear matrix-associated transcriptional factor, SATB2 exhibits aberrant expression in a variety of cancers and plays an important role in promoting tumor progression [17][18][19][20]39 . However, the posttranslational regulation of STAB2 is still poorly understood. In the present study, we report that the USP10 is a deubiquitinase and DTX3L is an E3 ubiquitin ligase of SATB2. USP10 counteracts DTX3L-promoted ubiquitination to stabilize SATB2 protein through mutually exclusive interaction as well as opposing activities, thereby promoting GSC maintenance and GBM tumor growth. Inhibition of USP10 by a small molecule inhibitor suppressed tumor growth in mouse models, suggesting that targeting USP10 may have therapeutic potential (Fig. 9).

In GBM, SATB2 is highly expressed in tumor tissues and enriched in GSCs 19 . Consistently, we find that USP10 and DTX3L are also preferentially expressed by GSCs. Moreover, both USP10 and DTX3L are co-localized with SATB2 in human GBM tissues. These findings suggest that USP10 and DTX3L may play a role in regulating the stability of SATB2. We observe that the expression levels of USP10 are significantly higher than that of DTX3L, which may account for the robust expression of SATB2 observed in GSCs. play a role in regulating SATB2. FOXM1 is a pivotal target gene of SATB2, playing a crucial role in mediating SATB2's regulation of GSC maintenance 19 . Consistently, our findings indicate that knockdown of USP10 or overexpression of DTX3L in GSCs significantly decreased FOXM1 expression and cell proliferation. These results further substantiate that USP10 and DTX3L exert their regulatory effects on GSC functions via the SATB2-FOXM1 axis. SOX2 is known to play a critical role in maintaining GSC stemness, and its downregulation has been shown to promote GSC differentiation 43,44 . Our previous work has shown that silencing SATB2 reduces SOX2 protein levels in GSCs 19 . Therefore, we speculate that USP10 inhibition or DTX3L overexpression may promote GSC differentiation by reducing SATB2 protein levels, although the underlying mechanism warrants further investigation. USP10 has been shown to promote the deubiquitination of several key factors, including FLT3, SIRT6, YAP/TAZ and P53, in various type of cancers 29,[45][46][47] . Further investigation is warranted to determine whether these factors are also subject to regulation by USP10 in GSCs. However, we have identified SATB2 as a substrate of USP10 in GSCs, and overexpression of SATB2 largely rescued the impaired GSC self-renewal and GBM growth caused by USP10 disruption. These findings at least confirm that SATB2 is a crucial downstream target of USP10 in GSCs. DTX3L has been reported to promote the ubiquitination of cGAS and P53 in certain cancers 48,49 . In the case of GBM, our research indicates that DTX3L inhibits GSC self-renewal and tumor growth primarily by modulating the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2. It remains unclear whether cGAS, P53 or other factors are also targeted for ubiquitination by DTX3L in GSCs. Nevertheless, we speculate that the regulatory mechanisms might differ across different cell types. Given the high expression of USP10 in GSCs, we explored the mechanism of increased USP10 transcription in GSCs. Although the downstream targets of USP10 have been well characterized in various cell types, the upstream factors that control USP10 expression remain largely unexplored. Our study demonstrates that transcription factor YY2 can stimulate USP10 transcription by binding to its promoter region. The enrichment of YY2 in GSCs within GBM further supports the notion that YY2 acts an upstream regulator of USP10. Previous studies have demonstrated that 1-5 μM Wu-5 had no effect on USP10 protein levels, while 10 μM markedly reduced USP10 protein levels in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and breast cancer cells 37,38 . Our results revealed that both USP10 and SATB2 levels decreased in a time-dependent manner following treatment with 16 μM Wu-5, with an initial reduction at 12 hours and further progressive declines at 24, 36, and 48 hours. Moreover, treatment with 8 and 16 μM Wu-5 for 24 hours dosedependently reduced USP10 and SATB2 protein levels, whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4 μM) had no significant impact on either protein. These findings indicate that USP10 and SATB2 protein levels decrease in parallel in a dose-and time-dependent manner upon Wu-5 treatment in GSCs. Cell viability assay also revealed that 8 and 16 μM Wu-5 dose-dependently inhibited GSC growth, whereas lower concentrations (2 and 4 μM) showed no significant effect. Previous study has demonstrated that Wu-5 exhibits inhibitory activity at low micromolar concentrations (1.5-3 μM) 37 . However, the lower concentrations tested (2 and 4 μM) proved ineffective in our GSC model, likely because USP10 protein levels showed no reduction under these conditions. Our results suggest that the reduction in USP10 protein levels, rather than mere enzymatic inhibition without affecting protein abundance, is likely the primary mechanism driving SATB2 degradation and the subsequent inhibition of GSC growth induced by effective concentrations of Wu-5. Since the inhibition of USP10 by Wu-5 has been shown to effectively suppress GBM tumor growth, targeting USP10 could present a promising therapeutic approach to improve GBM treatment. Considering that USP10 also promotes the progression of several other cancer types [27][28][29] , the use of Wu-5 to target USP10 may potentially improve treatments for a variety of tumors.

In summary, we have identified that the deubiquitinase USP10 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX3L function act in concert to regulate the ubiquitination and stability of SATB2, thereby controlling the maintenance of GSC and tumor growth. Targeting SATB2 stability through pharmacological inhibition of USP10 could represent a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance the efficacy of treatments for GBM.

For the identification of SATB2 binding proteins, peptides from both the experimental group and a control IgG group were extracted and separated. The peptides separated by liquid phase chromatography were ionized by a nanoESI source and then passed to a tandem mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Fusion Lumos, Thermo Fisher) for DDA (data-dependent acquisition) mode detection. The main parameters were set as follows: ion source voltage, 2 kV; MS1 scanning range, 350-1500 m/z; MS1 resolution, 60,000; MS2 starting m/z, 100; MS2 resolution, 15,000. The ion screening conditions for MS2 fragmentation were: charge 2+ to 6 +, and the top 30 parent ions with the peak intensity exceeding 20,000. The ion fragmentation mode was HCD, and the fragment ions were detected in the Orbitrap. The dynamic exclusion time was set to 30 s. The AGC was set to 1E5 for MS1 and 2E4 for MS2. For protein identification, experimental MS/MS data were matched against theoretical MS/MS data from a protein database. The raw MS data were converted into a peak list and searched against the UniProt database using Mascot (version 2.3.02). The search was performed using an mgf file as input against a pre-constructed database. The Mascot parameters were set as follows: Enzyme: Trypsin; Peptide mass tolerance: 10 ppm; Fragment mass tolerance: 0.02 Da; Fixed modifications: Carbamidomethyl (C); Variable modifications: Oxidation (M), Gln->pyro-Glu (N-term Q), Deamidated (NQ), Phospho (ST), Phospho (Y); Max missed cleavages: 1; Instrument type: ESI-FTICR. The search results were pre-processed and rescored using Percolator to improve the matching accuracy. The output was then filtered at a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) at the spectral level (PSM-level FDR ≤ 0.01) to obtain a list of significantly identified spectra and peptides.

div.head: Mass spectrometry analysis
div.p: For the identification of ubiquitinated sites on SATB2, peptides from both the experimental group and a control IgG group were extracted. The peptide samples were then separated and analyzed by a Q-Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) operating in DDA mode. The total analysis time was 60 min in positive ion mode. The full scan MS1 spectra were collected over the m/z range of 350-1800 with a resolution of 60,000 at 200 m/z, an AGC target of 3e6, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. For MS2 acquisition, the top 20 most intense precursor ions from each full scan were selected for fragmentation. The MS2 spectra were acquired with a resolution of 15,000 at 200 m/z, an AGC target of 1e5, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. HCD was used as the fragmentation mode with an isolation window of 1.6 m/z and a normalized collision energy of 28. For protein identification, experimental MS/MS data were matched against theoretical MS/MS data from a protein database. The raw MS data were searched against the UniProt database using MaxQuant (version 2.4.14.0). The Max-Quant parameters were set as follows: Enzyme: Trypsin; Precursor Tolerance (main search): 4.5 ppm; Precursor Tolerance (first search): 20 ppm; MS/MS tolerance: 20 ppm; Fixed modifications: Carbamidomethyl (C); Variable modifications: Oxidation (M), Acetyl (Protein Nterm), GlyGly (K). After database searching, the mass spectrometry data were filtered using the following criteria: PSM FDR ≤ 0.01, Site FDR ≤ 0.01, and Protein FDR ≤ 0.01 for peptide, modification site, and protein identification, respectively. To ensure the quality of modified peptide identifications, additional filters were applied, including a Modified Peptide Score ≥ 40 and the presence of at least one unmodified peptide (Unmodified peptides ≥ 0). A modification site was considered confidently localized when its localization probability was ≥ 0.75.

div.head: Intracranial tumor formation and treatment
div.p: BALB/c-Nude mice were purchased from Hunan Slack Jingda Experimental Animal (Changsha, China). Male or female BALB/c nude mice at 6-7 weeks were used and housed in the animal facility of the laboratory animal center at Huazhong Agricultural University. Mice were maintained at 22-24 °C and 40-70% humidity with a 12 h light/12 h dark schedule. Sex was not incorporated into the study design or analysis, as investigating potential sex-specific effects was outside the scope of this research. 50,000 GSCs were implanted into the right cerebral cortex at a depth of 3.5 mm to establish intracranial xenografts. Mice were maintained until neurological signs appeared (survival analysis). Neurological signs included hunched posture, gait changes, lethargy, and weight loss. For the drug treatment, Wu-5 (7.5 mg/kg; TargetMol, Cat# T77763) was dissolved in DMSO (Santa Cruz, sc-358801). 7 days post-GSC transplantation, mice were treated with Wu-5 or vehicle control 6 days per week and maintained until the appearance of neurological signs (survival analysis). The maximum tumor burden permitted by the ethics committee is 1.2 cm in diameter for mice, and the tumor weight must not exceed 10% of the body weight. No animals exceeded these limits in this study.

div.head: Statistics and reproducibility
div.p: All data are presented as the mean ± SD from at least three samples or experiments per data point. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test was used to evaluate the statistical significance for two groups. One-way ANOVA analysis followed by Tukey's test was used to examine the statistical significance for more than two groups. For quantification with two groups and the groups with subgroups, two-way ANOVA analysis followed by Sidak's test was used to evaluate statistical significance. For quantification with more than two groups and the groups with subgroups, two-way ANOVA analysis followed by Tukey's test was used to evaluate statistical significance. Data were normally distributed. A log-rank test was used to determine the statistical significance of Kaplan-Meier survival curves. For all statistical tests, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Precise experimental details are described in the figure legends.
